title: General Chemistry II
subject: Chemistry

cards.prompt: What is Electron-Domain Geometry? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: VSEPR electron-domain geometry is the arrangement of bonding domains and lone pairs around a central atom that approximately minimizes their mutual repulsion. A single, double, or triple bond counts as one domain. Two through six domains give linear, trigonal-planar, tetrahedral, trigonal-bipyramidal, and octahedral ideal arrangements.
required_concepts: Count each bond and each lone pair as one domain.
Geometry describes all domains around the central atom.
accepted_variants: Electron-pair-domain arrangement predicted by valence-shell repulsion.
major_error_concepts: Counting a double bond as two separate domains.
Ignoring lone pairs when assigning electron-domain geometry.

cards.prompt: What is Molecular Geometry? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Molecular geometry describes the spatial arrangement of atoms around a central atom, excluding lone pairs from the shape's name. Lone pairs still influence the arrangement: water has tetrahedral electron-domain geometry but bent molecular geometry.
required_concepts: Describes atom positions, not all electron domains.
Lone pairs affect shape even though they are not counted as atoms.
accepted_variants: The shape of the bonded-atom arrangement.
major_error_concepts: Calling water tetrahedral molecular geometry because it has four electron domains.

cards.prompt: What is Bond Energy? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Bond dissociation energy is the energy required to break a specified bond homolytically in an isolated gaseous species. Bond breaking absorbs energy; forming the same bond in the reverse process releases it. Tabulated mean bond enthalpies average over different molecular environments.
required_concepts: Breaking a bond requires energy.
Specify the bond and gaseous molecular environment, or recognize a tabulated average.
accepted_variants: Energy needed for gas-phase homolytic bond cleavage.
major_error_concepts: Saying bond breaking releases energy.

cards.prompt: What is Partial Pressure? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A component's partial pressure in an ideal-gas mixture is the pressure it would exert alone at the mixture's temperature and total volume: p_i = n_iRT/V.
required_concepts: Component pressure evaluated at the common mixture temperature and volume.
accepted_variants: Pressure contribution associated with one ideal-gas component.
major_error_concepts: Assigning every component the entire mixture pressure.

cards.prompt: What is Mole Fraction? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Mole fraction is the amount of one component divided by the total amount of all components: x_i = n_i/n_total. It is dimensionless, lies between zero and one, and the component mole fractions sum to one.
required_concepts: Ratio of component moles to total moles.
Dimensionless with fractions summing to one.
accepted_variants: Fraction of the total particle amount attributable to a component.
major_error_concepts: Equating mole fraction with mass fraction in every mixture.

cards.prompt: What is Dalton's Law? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Dalton's law states that the total pressure of an ideal-gas mixture equals the sum of its component partial pressures: P = sum p_i. Consequently p_i = x_iP for that mixture.
required_concepts: Total pressure is the sum of component partial pressures.
Ideal-mixture condition.
accepted_variants: Additive partial pressures of nonreacting ideal-gas components.
major_error_concepts: Adding component volumes instead of their partial pressures at the common volume.

cards.prompt: What is Standard State? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A thermodynamic standard state is a conventional reference state at a specified temperature and standard pressure, usually 1 bar. For gases the reference is the ideal gas at that pressure; for pure liquids and solids it is the pure substance. A standard state does not inherently require 0 degrees Celsius.
required_concepts: Reference state at specified temperature and standard pressure.
Not synonymous with STP.
accepted_variants: Conventional reference for thermodynamic quantities, with temperature stated separately.
major_error_concepts: Claiming the standard-state symbol fixes temperature to 273.15 K.

cards.prompt: What is Thermodynamic System? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A thermodynamic system is the part of the universe selected for analysis, separated conceptually from its surroundings by a boundary. The boundary determines which transfers of matter and energy are included in the analysis.
required_concepts: Chosen region or material under study.
Its boundary defines transfers to and from surroundings.
accepted_variants: The explicitly defined object of thermodynamic accounting.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every system must be sealed and isolated.

cards.prompt: What is Surroundings? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The surroundings are everything outside the chosen thermodynamic system that may interact with it. Heat or work gained by one side of a closed system-surroundings accounting boundary is lost by the other.
required_concepts: Outside the chosen system boundary.
Exchange depends on how the boundary is defined.
accepted_variants: The environment external to the system being analyzed.
major_error_concepts: Treating a calorimeter as always inside the reacting system regardless of the chosen boundary.

cards.prompt: What is State Function? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A state function is a property whose change depends only on the initial and final equilibrium states, not on the path connecting them. Internal energy and enthalpy are state functions; heat and work are process-dependent transfers.
required_concepts: Endpoint dependence rather than path dependence.
Distinguish state properties from transferred heat and work.
accepted_variants: A thermodynamic property with path-independent changes.
major_error_concepts: Calling heat a state function because energy is conserved.

cards.prompt: What is Heat? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Heat is energy transferred across a system boundary because of a temperature difference. Heat is a transfer, not a substance stored in an object; in the chemistry convention q is positive when the system absorbs heat.
required_concepts: Energy transfer caused by temperature difference.
Positive q means heat enters the system.
accepted_variants: Thermal energy transfer between system and surroundings.
major_error_concepts: Equating heat with temperature.
Calling an object's internal energy its stored heat.

cards.prompt: What is Work? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Work is energy transferred by a generalized force acting through a displacement rather than by a temperature difference. In chemistry's sign convention work done on the system is positive; pressure-volume work is w = -integral P_ext dV.
required_concepts: Energy transfer distinct from heat.
Work on the system is positive; expansion against positive external pressure gives negative work.
accepted_variants: Mechanical or other nonthermal energy transfer across a boundary.
major_error_concepts: Assigning positive work to expansion under the stated chemistry convention.

cards.prompt: What is Internal Energy? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Internal energy U is a state function describing a system's microscopic energy. For a closed system the first law in the chemistry sign convention is delta U = q + w, where q and w are positive for energy entering the system.
required_concepts: U is a state function.
Closed-system change equals heat plus work with stated signs.
accepted_variants: Microscopic system energy governed by delta U = q + w.
major_error_concepts: Saying internal energy equals heat transferred in every process.

cards.prompt: What is Enthalpy? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Enthalpy is the state function H = U + PV. For a closed system at constant pressure with only pressure-volume work, its change equals heat absorbed by the system: delta H = q_p.
required_concepts: H = U + PV.
Equality to heat requires constant pressure and only PV work.
major_error_concepts: Claiming enthalpy always equals heat or that delta H equals delta U in every process.

cards.prompt: What is Endothermic Process? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An endothermic process absorbs heat into the system, so q is positive. Under constant-pressure conditions with only PV work, the process has positive enthalpy change.
required_concepts: Heat enters the system.
Positive delta H under the stated constant-pressure conditions.
major_error_concepts: Identifying endothermic with every process whose system temperature increases.

cards.prompt: What is Exothermic Process? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An exothermic process releases heat from the system to its surroundings, so q is negative. Under constant-pressure conditions with only PV work, its enthalpy change is negative.
required_concepts: Heat leaves the system.
Negative delta H under the stated conditions.
major_error_concepts: Saying exothermic means heat enters the system.

cards.prompt: What is Specific Heat Capacity? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Specific heat capacity c is the heat needed per unit mass for a unit temperature increase under stated conditions. When c is approximately constant and no phase change occurs, q = mc delta T.
required_concepts: Heat capacity per unit mass.
Use q = mc delta T without phase change and with approximately constant c.
accepted_variants: Energy per mass per temperature increment, such as J g^-1 K^-1.
major_error_concepts: Omitting mass when using a specific heat capacity.

cards.prompt: What is Heat Capacity? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Heat capacity C is the heat required to raise the temperature of a specified object or system by one unit under stated conditions. For approximately constant C, q = C delta T; unlike specific heat capacity, C is not expressed per unit mass.
required_concepts: Applies to the whole specified object.
q = C delta T under suitable conditions.
accepted_variants: Energy per temperature change for the complete sample.
major_error_concepts: Confusing J/K with J/(g K).

cards.prompt: What is Calorimetry? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Calorimetry measures heat transfer using observed temperature changes and known heat capacities. With negligible exchange to the external environment, heat lost by the reaction or hot body equals heat gained by the other included components.
required_concepts: Infer heat transfer from temperature changes and heat capacities.
Account for all included components using energy conservation.
accepted_variants: Measurement of exchanged heat by thermal accounting.
major_error_concepts: Ignoring the apparatus heat capacity when it is appreciable.

cards.prompt: What is Thermochemical Equation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A thermochemical equation is a balanced chemical equation accompanied by the enthalpy change for the reaction as written, including physical states. Reversing the equation reverses the enthalpy sign; multiplying its coefficients multiplies the associated enthalpy change.
required_concepts: Balanced equation with physical states and associated delta H.
Reaction scaling and reversal also transform delta H.
accepted_variants: A chemical reaction equation with its corresponding heat-of-reaction information.
major_error_concepts: Keeping delta H unchanged after doubling every reaction coefficient.

cards.prompt: What is Enthalpy Change? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Enthalpy change is delta H = H_final - H_initial. For a reaction under stated conditions it compares the enthalpy of products with reactants for specified amounts and physical states; its sign distinguishes heat absorption from release under constant-pressure PV-work conditions.
required_concepts: Final minus initial enthalpy.
Reaction amounts and physical states matter.
accepted_variants: Difference in the enthalpy state function between two states.
major_error_concepts: Calling delta H an absolute enthalpy value.

cards.prompt: What is Hess's Law? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Hess's law states that the enthalpy change of an overall reaction equals the sum of the enthalpy changes of any component reactions that add to it. This works because enthalpy is a state function, not because the reaction physically follows those steps.
required_concepts: Add enthalpy changes for reactions that sum to the target reaction.
Path independence follows from enthalpy being a state function.
accepted_variants: Reaction enthalpies add algebraically with their balanced equations.
major_error_concepts: Requiring the algebraic component reactions to be the actual reaction mechanism.

cards.prompt: What is Internal Energy, Enthalpy, and Heat? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Internal energy U and enthalpy H = U + PV are state functions; heat q is path-dependent energy transfer. For a closed system with only PV work, q equals delta U at constant volume and delta H at constant pressure under the respective constraints.
required_concepts: U and H are state functions; q is a transfer.
Distinguish constant-volume and constant-pressure heat relations.
accepted_variants: Heat can equal a state-function change only under specified process conditions.
major_error_concepts: Treating U, H, and q as interchangeable names for the same quantity.

cards.prompt: What is Bond-Enthalpy Estimates? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A reaction enthalpy can be estimated as the sum of mean bond enthalpies for bonds broken minus those for bonds formed. Mean bond enthalpies are gas-phase averages, so the estimate neglects detailed molecular environment and may need phase-change corrections.
required_concepts: Bonds broken minus bonds formed.
Gas-phase averages give estimates, not exact reaction enthalpies.
accepted_variants: Energy input for cleavage minus energy released by bond formation.
major_error_concepts: Reversing the subtraction.
Applying gas-phase averages as exact values for arbitrary liquid or solid reactions.

cards.prompt: What is Intermolecular Force? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Intermolecular forces are interactions between distinct molecules or particles rather than the covalent bonds within a molecule. They influence phase behavior and physical properties, with strength depending on charge distribution, separation, and polarizability.
required_concepts: Interactions between particles.
Distinguish them from intramolecular covalent bonds.
major_error_concepts: Claiming boiling ordinary molecular water primarily breaks its O-H covalent bonds.

cards.prompt: What is London Dispersion? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: London dispersion arises from correlated fluctuations in electronic charge distributions that create attractive interactions. It occurs in all atoms and molecules and often increases with polarizability and favorable contact area.
required_concepts: Fluctuating correlated electron distributions.
Present even in nonpolar species.
accepted_variants: Dispersion attraction from instantaneous induced dipoles.
major_error_concepts: Claiming nonpolar particles experience no attractive interactions.

cards.prompt: What is Dipole–Dipole Interaction? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Dipole-dipole interactions occur between permanent molecular dipoles. Their energy depends on orientation and separation, so molecular polarity contributes to bulk behavior without determining it alone.
required_concepts: Interaction of permanent dipoles.
Orientation matters.
major_error_concepts: Treating every encounter of two dipoles as equally attractive regardless of orientation.

cards.prompt: What is Hydrogen Bond? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A hydrogen bond is a directional interaction involving a hydrogen bonded to an electronegative donor and an electron-rich acceptor. Common introductory examples use N, O, or F donors, but the broader concept is not restricted to that mnemonic alone.
required_concepts: Donor-bound hydrogen interacts with an acceptor.
Direction and chemical context matter.
major_error_concepts: Calling every bond containing hydrogen a hydrogen bond.

cards.prompt: What is Ion–Dipole Interaction? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An ion-dipole interaction is the attraction or repulsion between an ion and a permanent molecular dipole. Favorable orientations help stabilize dissolved ions in polar solvents.
required_concepts: Ion interacting with a permanent dipole.
Solvent orientation can stabilize ions.
major_error_concepts: Calling an interaction between two neutral permanent dipoles ion-dipole.

cards.prompt: What is Vapor Pressure? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Equilibrium vapor pressure is the pressure of vapor coexisting with its condensed phase at a specified temperature. It reflects the dynamic balance of evaporation and condensation and rises with temperature for ordinary liquid-vapor coexistence.
required_concepts: Vapor pressure at phase equilibrium and stated temperature.
Not determined solely by the container's amount when both phases remain.
major_error_concepts: Assuming doubling the liquid amount necessarily doubles its equilibrium vapor pressure at fixed temperature.

cards.prompt: What is Boiling Point? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A liquid boils when its equilibrium vapor pressure equals the surrounding pressure, allowing vapor bubbles to grow within it. Its boiling temperature therefore depends on external pressure.
required_concepts: Vapor pressure equals external pressure.
Boiling point is pressure-dependent.
accepted_variants: Temperature of bulk vapor formation at the stated pressure.
major_error_concepts: Treating boiling point as independent of atmospheric or applied pressure.

cards.prompt: What is Phase Diagram? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A phase diagram maps stable phases and coexistence boundaries against variables such as temperature and pressure. Crossing a boundary changes the equilibrium phase under the diagram's composition and other assumptions.
required_concepts: Regions and boundaries of phase stability.
State the axes and fixed composition.
accepted_variants: A map of equilibrium phase behavior.
major_error_concepts: Interpreting a phase boundary as an arbitrary kinetic reaction-rate curve.

cards.prompt: What is Triple Point? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A triple point is the temperature-pressure condition at which three phases of a substance coexist in equilibrium. It is a specific coexistence condition rather than an entire region of three independently variable phases.
required_concepts: Three phases coexist at the specified condition.
major_error_concepts: Confusing the triple point with the liquid-vapor critical endpoint.

cards.prompt: What is Critical Point? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The liquid-vapor critical point ends the coexistence curve where the distinction between liquid and gas disappears. Above it, a supercritical fluid cannot be separated into ordinary liquid and vapor by crossing that vanished boundary.
required_concepts: Endpoint of liquid-vapor distinction.
Different from a triple point.
major_error_concepts: Claiming a supercritical fluid consists of a visible liquid layer under a separate gas layer at equilibrium.

cards.prompt: What is Crystalline Solid? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A crystalline solid has long-range ordered particle arrangement, unlike an amorphous solid's lack of the same periodic order. Crystal structure and bonding together determine many material properties.
required_concepts: Long-range structural order.
major_error_concepts: Defining crystallinity solely by whether a sample is transparent.

cards.prompt: What is Unit Cell? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A unit cell is a repeating geometrical region used to generate a crystal lattice by translation. Atoms on shared boundaries contribute fractions to the cell's particle count.
required_concepts: Translational repeating cell.
Account for sharing of boundary particles.
accepted_variants: A building block of a periodic crystal description.
major_error_concepts: Counting every corner atom as entirely contained in one cell.

cards.prompt: What is Solid Structure Types? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Molecular, ionic, metallic, and covalent-network solids differ in constituent particles and dominant bonding. These distinctions help explain conductivity, hardness, and melting behavior, though actual materials can combine features.
required_concepts: Distinguish major solid types by particles and bonding.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every solid is made of separate discrete molecules.

cards.prompt: What is Solution? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A solution is a homogeneous mixture on the molecular or ionic scale, with components often designated solvent and solutes. Solutions can occur in phases other than liquids.
required_concepts: Homogeneous mixture.
Not limited to aqueous liquids.
major_error_concepts: Defining every mixture with visible suspended particles as a true solution.

cards.prompt: What is Solvation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Solvation is stabilization and organization of solvent around dissolved particles through intermolecular interactions. Hydration is solvation by water; dissolution depends on the full energetic and entropic balance, not solvation attraction alone.
required_concepts: Solvent interaction with dissolved species.
Hydration is the water-specific case.
major_error_concepts: Assuming favorable solvation alone guarantees unlimited solubility.

cards.prompt: What is Solubility? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Solubility is the equilibrium amount or concentration of a solute that can dissolve under specified conditions. Temperature, pressure for gases, solvent composition, and reaction chemistry can affect it.
required_concepts: Equilibrium dissolved limit under stated conditions.
accepted_variants: The saturation concentration or corresponding amount.
major_error_concepts: Equating solubility with how quickly a solid dissolves.

cards.prompt: What is Saturated Solution? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A saturated solution is at the equilibrium solubility limit for a specified solute under the current conditions. When excess solid is present, dissolution and crystallization can continue at equal net rates.
required_concepts: At the equilibrium dissolution limit.
Dynamic exchange can persist.
major_error_concepts: Claiming particles stop exchanging between solid and solution at saturation.

cards.prompt: What is Supersaturated Solution? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A supersaturated solution contains more dissolved solute than the equilibrium solubility under its current conditions. It is metastable and may precipitate when nucleation occurs.
required_concepts: Concentration exceeds the equilibrium limit.
Metastability rather than a new equilibrium solubility.
major_error_concepts: Treating supersaturation as proof that the tabulated equilibrium solubility is irrelevant.

cards.prompt: What is Molarity? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Molarity is moles of solute per liter of solution. Because solution volume can vary with temperature, molarity can change even when solute amount stays fixed.
required_concepts: Moles divided by total solution volume.
Not solvent volume.
major_error_concepts: Using liters of solvent alone as the denominator by definition.

cards.prompt: What is Molality? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Molality is moles of solute per kilogram of solvent. Its mass-based denominator differs from molarity's solution-volume denominator and does not expand thermally like a volume.
required_concepts: Moles per kilogram of solvent.
major_error_concepts: Using kilograms of the entire solution instead of solvent mass.

cards.prompt: What is Dilution Relation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For dilution with conserved solute and no reaction or loss, initial concentration times initial solution volume equals final concentration times final volume when concentration is amount per volume. This expresses solute conservation, not universal volume additivity.
required_concepts: Conserved solute amount gives C1V1=C2V2.
Final volume need not equal naive added component volumes.
major_error_concepts: Applying the relation across a reaction consuming solute without accounting for it.

cards.prompt: What is Henry's Law? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Henry's law states that the dissolved concentration of a dilute gas is proportional to its partial pressure above the liquid at fixed temperature under the applicable conditions. Constants have different reciprocal conventions, so the chosen equation and units must be stated.
required_concepts: Dilute dissolved gas proportional to partial pressure.
Specify temperature and constant convention.
major_error_concepts: Treating all published Henry constants as interchangeable numbers with identical units.

cards.prompt: What is Raoult's Law? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Raoult's law gives a component's equilibrium vapor partial pressure as its liquid mole fraction times its pure-component vapor pressure for an ideal solution. The relation uses the same temperature for both vapor pressures.
required_concepts: p_i=x_i p_i star in an ideal solution.
Liquid mole fraction and temperature consistency.
major_error_concepts: Using solute mass fraction in place of liquid mole fraction without conversion.

cards.prompt: What is Ideal Solution? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An ideal solution obeys the ideal mixing chemical-potential relation; in elementary terms its components obey Raoult's law over the applicable composition range. Ideal mixing has zero enthalpy and volume change in the standard model.
required_concepts: Ideal mixing behavior rather than arbitrary real-solution behavior.
Zero ideal mixing enthalpy and volume change.
accepted_variants: A solution with ideal component activities equal to mole fractions.
major_error_concepts: Assuming all dilute and concentrated real solutions are ideal.

cards.prompt: What is Colligative Property? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Colligative properties depend primarily on the number of dissolved particles relative to solvent in the dilute ideal limit. Examples include vapor-pressure lowering, boiling-point elevation, freezing-point depression, and osmotic pressure.
required_concepts: Depend on particle concentration in the stated limit.
Chemical identity can matter through dissociation and nonideality.
major_error_concepts: Claiming the same mass of every solute produces identical colligative effects.

cards.prompt: What is Van 't Hoff Factor? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The van 't Hoff factor i represents the effective number of solute particles contributing per dissolved formula unit in an elementary colligative model. Dissociation, association, and nonideal interactions can make it differ from a simple integer prediction.
required_concepts: Effective particle-number factor.
Observed values need not equal ideal dissociation counts.
major_error_concepts: Assuming an electrolyte's i is exactly its stoichiometric ion count at every concentration.

cards.prompt: What is Boiling-Point Elevation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For a dilute solution of a nonvolatile solute, boiling-point elevation is approximated by delta T_b=i K_b m, where m is molality and K_b is the solvent constant. This relies on the appropriate dilute colligative assumptions.
required_concepts: Elevation proportional to effective molality.
Nonvolatile-solute and dilute assumptions.
major_error_concepts: Using molarity instead of molality without a justified approximation.

cards.prompt: What is Freezing-Point Depression? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For a dilute solution under the standard freezing model, freezing-point depression is delta T_f=i K_f m. It describes how solute lowers the solvent's freezing temperature relative to the pure solvent.
required_concepts: Freezing temperature decreases.
Effective molality relation.
major_error_concepts: Adding delta T_f to the pure-solvent freezing temperature when the defined delta is a positive depression magnitude.

cards.prompt: What is Osmotic Pressure? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Osmotic pressure is the pressure difference needed to prevent net solvent flow through an ideal semipermeable membrane between a solution and a reference solvent. A dilute ideal solute model gives Pi=i M R T.
required_concepts: Pressure needed to balance osmotic solvent tendency.
Dilute ideal relation uses absolute temperature.
accepted_variants: The pressure equivalent of osmotic driving force.
major_error_concepts: Assuming osmosis requires solute particles to pass freely through the semipermeable membrane.

cards.prompt: What is Reaction Rate? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Reaction rate measures composition change per time, with stoichiometric normalization giving one reaction-rate convention across species. Reactant disappearance rates use a minus sign, while product formation rates use a plus sign.
required_concepts: Composition change per time.
Normalize by stoichiometric coefficients and signs.
accepted_variants: The speed of a reaction expressed through species change.
major_error_concepts: Equating raw disappearance rates of differently weighted reactants without their coefficients.

cards.prompt: What is Rate Law? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A rate law relates reaction rate to concentrations or activities and a rate coefficient under specified conditions. Its exponents are determined by mechanism or experiment and are not generally the balanced overall reaction coefficients.
required_concepts: Rate dependence on reacting conditions.
Overall stoichiometry does not generally determine exponents.
major_error_concepts: Reading all rate-law powers directly from a non-elementary overall equation.

cards.prompt: What is Reaction Order? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Reaction order with respect to a species is its concentration exponent in a power-law rate expression; overall order is the sum of those exponents. Orders can be zero, fractional, or negative and may be only locally applicable.
required_concepts: Exponent-based kinetic dependence.
Not necessarily a positive integer.
accepted_variants: The concentration-power order of a rate law.
major_error_concepts: Equating order with the number of reactants in every overall reaction.

cards.prompt: What is Rate Constant? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The rate constant is the proportionality factor in a specified rate law at stated conditions. Its units depend on the overall reaction order, and its value commonly changes with temperature or catalyst environment.
required_concepts: Coefficient of the stated rate law.
Units depend on order and value depends on conditions.
major_error_concepts: Confusing the rate constant k with the equilibrium constant K.

cards.prompt: What is Method of Initial Rates? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The method of initial rates compares rates measured near the start of runs with different initial concentrations. Varying concentrations in a controlled design can identify rate-law exponents without assuming they equal stoichiometric coefficients.
required_concepts: Compare initial rates under controlled concentration changes.
major_error_concepts: Changing several conditions unpredictably and attributing the entire rate change to one concentration.

cards.prompt: What is Zero-Order Integrated Rate Law? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For zero-order disappearance with rate k over its valid range, concentration follows [A]_t=[A]_0-k t. The linear law cannot continue into negative concentration after the reactant is exhausted.
required_concepts: Linear concentration decline at constant rate.
Finite validity before exhaustion.
major_error_concepts: Extending the formula to physically negative concentrations.

cards.prompt: What is First-Order Integrated Rate Law? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For first-order disappearance, [A]_t=[A]_0 exp(-k t), equivalently ln[A]_t=ln[A]_0-k t. The decay rate is proportional to the amount remaining.
required_concepts: Exponential concentration decay.
Log concentration has slope -k.
major_error_concepts: Treating first-order concentration as decreasing by an equal absolute amount each interval.

cards.prompt: What is Second-Order Integrated Rate Law? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For disappearance obeying -d[A]/dt=k[A]^2 under this rate convention, 1/[A]_t=1/[A]_0+k t. Other second-order mechanisms or reactant combinations require their corresponding integrated forms.
required_concepts: Reciprocal concentration is linear for the stated single-species law.
Rate convention and form matter.
major_error_concepts: Applying the same formula unchanged to every reaction whose overall order is two.

cards.prompt: What is Reaction Half-Life? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Reaction half-life is the time for a specified reactant concentration to fall to half its starting value. For first-order decay t_half=ln 2/k, independent of starting concentration; other orders generally differ.
required_concepts: Time to halve the specified concentration.
Concentration-independent formula is first-order-specific.
accepted_variants: The halving time of a reactant.
major_error_concepts: Assuming all reaction orders share a constant half-life.

cards.prompt: What is Arrhenius Equation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The Arrhenius equation k=A exp(-E_a/(RT)) models temperature dependence of a rate constant. The prefactor and apparent activation energy can depend on mechanism and regime, so one fit need not apply over every temperature range.
required_concepts: Exponential temperature dependence with absolute T.
Model parameters and regime matter.
major_error_concepts: Using Celsius directly in the exponential denominator.

cards.prompt: What is Activation Energy? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Activation energy characterizes the temperature sensitivity or effective barrier associated with a reaction pathway in the model used. It is not the overall enthalpy difference between products and reactants.
required_concepts: Barrier-related or Arrhenius temperature-sensitivity quantity.
Distinct from reaction enthalpy.
major_error_concepts: Equating activation energy with delta H of the complete reaction.

cards.prompt: What is Collision Theory? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Collision theory connects reaction rate to encounter frequency and the fraction of encounters with suitable energy and orientation. A collision is not automatically a successful reaction event.
required_concepts: Encounters need appropriate energy and geometry.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every molecular collision produces products.

cards.prompt: What is Transition State? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A transition state is the high-free-energy configuration region along a reaction pathway separating reactant-like and product-like states. It is not an ordinary isolable intermediate at a stable local minimum.
required_concepts: Barrier configuration rather than stable intermediate.
major_error_concepts: Treating a transition state as a bottleable stable reaction intermediate.

cards.prompt: What is Catalyst? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A catalyst changes the reaction pathway to increase the rate of approach to equilibrium while being regenerated overall. It does not change the equilibrium constant for the same reaction at the same temperature.
required_concepts: Alternative kinetic pathway with catalyst regenerated.
No change to equilibrium thermodynamics.
accepted_variants: A reaction-rate accelerator not consumed in the net process.
major_error_concepts: Claiming a catalyst shifts the thermodynamic equilibrium toward products.

cards.prompt: What is Reaction Mechanism? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A reaction mechanism is a proposed sequence of elementary steps explaining the net reaction and observed kinetics. Matching the overall equation alone is insufficient evidence that a mechanism is correct.
required_concepts: Sequence of elementary events.
Must be compatible with kinetics and other evidence.
accepted_variants: A molecular pathway for the reaction.
major_error_concepts: Calling the balanced overall equation a complete mechanism automatically.

cards.prompt: What is Elementary Step? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An elementary step represents a single modeled molecular event. Its molecularity counts participating reactant entities, and a simple mass-action rate expression can follow that elementary description under its assumptions.
required_concepts: Single modeled molecular event.
Molecularity differs from arbitrary overall reaction order.
major_error_concepts: Assigning fractional molecularity to one elementary collision event because a fitted overall order is fractional.

cards.prompt: What is Reaction Intermediate? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A reaction intermediate is formed in one mechanistic step and consumed in another, so it cancels from the overall equation. It differs from a transition state and from a catalyst regenerated after participating.
required_concepts: Produced then consumed in the mechanism.
Absent from the net equation after cancellation.
major_error_concepts: Identifying every high-energy transition state as an intermediate.

cards.prompt: What is Rate-Determining-Step Approximation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A rate-determining-step approximation treats one sufficiently slow or controlling step as governing the overall rate under stated conditions. Other steps and intermediate concentrations still matter when deriving a rate law.
required_concepts: Dominant kinetic bottleneck is an approximation.
Upstream equilibria or intermediate supply can affect the result.
major_error_concepts: Reading the slow step's equation alone as the full observed rate law without eliminating intermediates.

cards.prompt: What is Steady-State Approximation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The steady-state approximation sets an intermediate's net accumulation rate approximately to zero because its production and consumption nearly balance over the relevant interval. Its concentration need not be zero, and the approximation is not necessarily thermodynamic equilibrium.
required_concepts: Intermediate production approximately balances consumption.
Steady concentration is not zero concentration or full equilibrium.
major_error_concepts: Setting the intermediate concentration itself to zero instead of its time derivative.

cards.prompt: What is Chemical Equilibrium? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Chemical equilibrium is a state with no net macroscopic reaction progress at fixed conditions because forward and reverse processes balance. Equilibrium composition depends on thermodynamic constraints, not solely on how fast equilibrium is reached.
required_concepts: No net composition change from the balanced reversible reaction.
Rate and equilibrium composition differ.
accepted_variants: The thermodynamic balance state of a reaction.
major_error_concepts: Defining equilibrium as equal concentrations of every reactant and product.

cards.prompt: What is Dynamic Equilibrium? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Dynamic equilibrium means opposing microscopic processes continue while their macroscopic effects cancel. For a reversible reaction, forward and reverse rates are equal even though individual molecules keep reacting.
required_concepts: Opposing rates equal, not both necessarily zero.
accepted_variants: Microscopic turnover without net macroscopic change.
major_error_concepts: Claiming all molecular reactions stop at equilibrium.

cards.prompt: What is Equilibrium Constant? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For a balanced reaction aA+bB <=> cC+dD, the thermodynamic equilibrium constant is K=(a_C^c a_D^d)/(a_A^a a_B^b) evaluated at equilibrium at the specified temperature and standard-state convention. Each a_i is a dimensionless activity. Pure condensed phases have unit activity under the usual pure-phase reference approximation. Reversing the written reaction replaces K by 1/K; K is not a rate constant.
required_concepts: At equilibrium divide product activities by reactant activities, each raised to its stoichiometric coefficient.
The balanced reaction, temperature and activity convention must be specified.
accepted_variants: K is the equilibrium value of the product-over-reactant activity quotient; for 2A <=> B, K=a_B/a_A^2.
major_error_concepts: Using reactants over products for the reaction as written.
Replacing stoichiometric powers by arbitrary reaction-order powers.
Confusing equilibrium composition with reaction speed.

cards.prompt: What is Reaction Quotient? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The reaction quotient Q uses the same activity expression as K but evaluates the current composition, whether or not equilibrium has been reached. Comparing Q with K predicts the direction of thermodynamic relaxation.
required_concepts: Current activity ratio with equilibrium-expression form.
major_error_concepts: Assuming Q equals K at every composition.

cards.term: Reaction Direction from Q and K
cards.prompt: What is Reaction Direction from Q and K? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For a reaction written in the forward direction, Q<K favors net forward progress and Q>K favors reverse progress toward equilibrium at fixed conditions. Q=K gives no thermodynamic driving force for net progress.
required_concepts: Correct forward/reverse comparison.
Reaction writing convention matters.
accepted_variants: Thermodynamic direction from the quotient-constant comparison.
major_error_concepts: Predicting faster kinetics solely because Q is far from K.

cards.prompt: What is Heterogeneous Equilibrium? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A heterogeneous equilibrium involves more than one phase. Pure solid and pure liquid activities are omitted as unit factors in the standard equilibrium expression while the phases are present; removing a phase can change the applicable equilibrium situation.
required_concepts: Multiple phases.
Unit activity does not mean a phase is irrelevant when absent.
major_error_concepts: Assuming the amount of a solid never matters even after the solid phase disappears.

cards.prompt: What is Kp and Kc Relation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For ideal gases in the common textbook pressure and concentration conventions, Kp=Kc(RT)^(delta n_gas), where delta n_gas is product gas stoichiometric sum minus reactant gas sum. Fully dimensionless definitions require consistent standard-state factors.
required_concepts: Gas mole-change exponent.
State conventions and units consistently.
accepted_variants: Ideal-gas conversion between pressure and concentration equilibrium expressions.
major_error_concepts: Counting solids in delta n_gas or mixing incompatible standard-state conventions.

cards.prompt: What is Combining Equilibrium Constants? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Reversing a reaction replaces K by 1/K; multiplying all coefficients by a factor raises K to that factor; adding reactions multiplies their equilibrium constants. These rules follow the activity expression or free-energy additivity.
required_concepts: Reverse reciprocates, scale exponentiates, add multiplies.
accepted_variants: Algebra of equilibrium constants under reaction manipulation.
major_error_concepts: Adding K values when adding reactions.

cards.prompt: What is Le Chatelier's Principle? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Le Chatelier's principle qualitatively predicts how an equilibrium responds to an imposed change by tending to oppose that disturbance. Precise predictions require specifying the constraints and can be obtained through Q and K rather than an unqualified slogan.
required_concepts: Qualitative response to a disturbance.
Fixed-volume versus fixed-pressure and temperature conditions matter.
major_error_concepts: Assuming adding inert gas always shifts every gas equilibrium regardless of constraints.

cards.prompt: What is ICE Table? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An ICE table organizes initial, change, and equilibrium amounts or concentrations for a reaction. Stoichiometry connects the changes, while the equilibrium expression and physical nonnegativity constrain the resulting unknown.
required_concepts: Initial-change-equilibrium bookkeeping.
Changes follow stoichiometric ratios.
major_error_concepts: Assigning equal changes to every species regardless of coefficients.

cards.prompt: What is Bronsted–Lowry Acid and Base? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A Bronsted-Lowry acid donates a proton and a Bronsted-Lowry base accepts one in the specified reaction. Acid-base behavior is relational and can depend on the partner and solvent.
required_concepts: Proton donor versus acceptor.
Context determines the role.
major_error_concepts: Defining every base only as a substance containing an OH group.

cards.prompt: What is Lewis Acid and Base? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A Lewis acid accepts an electron pair and a Lewis base donates one to form an interaction or bond. This framework includes many acid-base processes without proton transfer.
required_concepts: Electron-pair acceptor versus donor.
Broader than proton transfer.
major_error_concepts: Reversing the donor and acceptor roles.

cards.prompt: What is Conjugate Acid–Base Pair? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A conjugate acid-base pair differs by one proton. Donating a proton creates an acid's conjugate base; accepting a proton creates a base's conjugate acid.
required_concepts: Members differ by one proton.
Charge changes consistently with proton transfer.
accepted_variants: The paired forms connected by proton loss or gain.
major_error_concepts: Pairing species that differ by an electron rather than a proton as a Bronsted conjugate pair.

cards.prompt: What is Acid Strength versus Concentration? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Acid strength describes the tendency to transfer a proton in a specified solvent, while concentration describes how much acid is present per amount of solution. A dilute strong acid and a concentrated weak acid are both possible.
required_concepts: Extent or tendency of ionization differs from amount per volume.
accepted_variants: Strength is an equilibrium property; concentration is a composition measure.
major_error_concepts: Using strong and concentrated as interchangeable terms.

cards.prompt: What is Acid Dissociation Constant? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The acid dissociation constant Ka is the equilibrium constant for an acid transferring a proton to the solvent, conventionally water in introductory examples. Larger Ka generally means a stronger acid within a common solvent and temperature convention.
required_concepts: Acid-ionization equilibrium constant.
Compare strengths under common conditions.
major_error_concepts: Treating Ka as simply the starting acid concentration.

cards.prompt: What is Base Dissociation Constant? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The base dissociation constant Kb describes a base accepting a proton from the solvent, commonly producing hydroxide in water. It measures equilibrium basicity under specified solvent and temperature conditions.
required_concepts: Equilibrium constant for base proton acceptance.
major_error_concepts: Assuming all bases have the same Kb because they generate hydroxide in water.

cards.prompt: What is Water Ion Product? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The water ion product Kw equals the product of hydrogen-ion and hydroxide-ion activities in the chosen aqueous convention. It depends on temperature; the familiar value near 10^-14 applies around 25 degrees Celsius, not at all temperatures.
required_concepts: Product of relevant ion activities.
Temperature-dependent.
major_error_concepts: Assuming Kw is exactly 10^-14 under every temperature and solution condition.

cards.prompt: What is pH? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: pH is the negative base-ten logarithm of hydrogen-ion activity. Replacing activity with molar concentration is a dilute-solution approximation; neutrality is determined relative to Kw rather than an invariant pH of seven at every temperature.
required_concepts: Negative log of hydrogen-ion activity.
Concentration approximation and temperature-dependent neutrality.
major_error_concepts: Defining pH universally as a number restricted to zero through fourteen.

cards.prompt: What is pOH? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: pOH is the negative base-ten logarithm of hydroxide-ion activity. In the corresponding aqueous activity convention, pH+pOH=pKw; the commonly used sum fourteen is temperature-specific.
required_concepts: Negative log hydroxide activity.
Sum with pH equals pKw.
major_error_concepts: Using pH+pOH=14 regardless of temperature.

cards.prompt: What is pKa? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: pKa is -log10 Ka. A smaller pKa corresponds to a larger acid dissociation constant and thus a stronger acid within a common comparison setting.
required_concepts: Negative logarithm of Ka.
Smaller pKa means stronger acid under matching conditions.
major_error_concepts: Claiming larger pKa always means stronger acidity.

cards.prompt: What is Conjugate Ka–Kb Relation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For a conjugate acid-base pair in water under consistent conventions, Ka times Kb equals Kw. Consequently a stronger acid has a weaker conjugate base relative to the same solvent system.
required_concepts: Ka Kb=Kw for a conjugate pair.
Use matching solvent and temperature.
accepted_variants: The reciprocal-strength relation for conjugate partners.
major_error_concepts: Multiplying Ka and Kb for unrelated species and assuming the result is Kw.

cards.prompt: What is Polyprotic Acid? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A polyprotic acid can donate more than one proton through successive equilibrium steps. Each step has its own dissociation constant, and the steps must not be treated as identical simultaneous ionizations.
required_concepts: Multiple stepwise proton donations.
Separate equilibrium constant for each step.
accepted_variants: An acid with multiple ionizable protons.
major_error_concepts: Using one Ka for every proton dissociation without an explicit approximation.

cards.prompt: What is Amphiprotic Species? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An amphiprotic species can either donate or accept a proton depending on its reaction partner. Water and hydrogen carbonate are common examples of this dual Bronsted behavior.
required_concepts: Can be proton donor or acceptor.
accepted_variants: A species with both Bronsted acid and base roles.
major_error_concepts: Defining amphiprotic solely as the ability to donate two protons.

cards.prompt: What is Salt Hydrolysis? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Salt hydrolysis occurs when dissolved salt ions react with water as acids or bases, altering the solution's hydrogen-ion balance. The pH depends on the acid-base properties of the ions rather than the fact that the starting solid is called a salt.
required_concepts: Ions react with water and affect acidity.
Salt solutions are not automatically neutral.
accepted_variants: Acid-base reactions of dissolved salt ions.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every salt dissolved in water produces pH seven.

cards.prompt: What is Common-Ion Effect? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The common-ion effect is the equilibrium shift caused by adding a species already present as an ion in that equilibrium. It commonly reduces weak-electrolyte ionization or salt solubility under suitable conditions.
required_concepts: Added shared ion alters an existing equilibrium.
Specific outcome depends on the equilibrium and conditions.
accepted_variants: Suppression by an ion common to the equilibrium.
major_error_concepts: Assuming a common ion changes the equilibrium constant itself at unchanged temperature.

cards.prompt: What is Buffer? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A buffer resists moderate pH changes through a reservoir of a weak acid and its conjugate base, or the analogous weak-base pair. It has finite capacity and works best over a limited range of component ratios.
required_concepts: Conjugate pair consumes added acid or base.
Resistance is limited, not perfect.
accepted_variants: An acid-base solution that moderates pH changes.
major_error_concepts: Claiming a buffer maintains exactly the same pH after any amount of added acid.

cards.prompt: What is Henderson–Hasselbalch Relation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The Henderson-Hasselbalch relation is pH=pKa+log10(a_base/a_acid) for a conjugate pair with consistent activities. Concentration ratios are often used as an approximation when solution conditions justify them.
required_concepts: pH equals pKa plus log conjugate-base/acid ratio.
Activity versus concentration distinction.
major_error_concepts: Reversing the base-to-acid ratio.

cards.prompt: What is Buffer Capacity? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Buffer capacity measures how much strong acid or base a buffer can absorb before a specified pH change. It depends on total buffer concentration and composition, not just the starting pH.
required_concepts: Amount of added acid/base tolerated per pH change.
Concentration and ratio both matter.
accepted_variants: The finite acid-base reserve of a buffer.
major_error_concepts: Assuming two buffers at identical pH necessarily have equal capacities.

cards.prompt: What is Acid–Base Titration? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An acid-base titration tracks the response as a known acid or base reacts with an unknown amount of its counterpart. Stoichiometry determines equivalence, while equilibrium chemistry determines the pH along the curve.
required_concepts: Known reagent amount probes unknown acid/base amount.
Stoichiometry and equilibrium have distinct roles.
major_error_concepts: Assuming stoichiometric equivalence alone fixes pH at seven for every titration.

cards.prompt: What is Equivalence Point? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The equivalence point is the point where added titrant has reacted in the stoichiometric amount required by the defined analyte reaction. Its pH depends on the acid-base system and is not universally neutral.
required_concepts: Stoichiometric completion for the specified reaction.
pH depends on chemistry.
major_error_concepts: Defining equivalence point by any visible color change irrespective of stoichiometry.

cards.prompt: What is Titration Endpoint? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An endpoint is an experimentally detected signal used to estimate the equivalence point, such as an indicator change. Endpoint and equivalence can differ, producing a systematic titration error.
required_concepts: Observed stopping or detection signal.
Not inherently identical to stoichiometric equivalence.
major_error_concepts: Treating every indicator endpoint as mathematically exact equivalence.

cards.prompt: What is Strong Acid–Strong Base Titration? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: In a strong acid-strong base titration, excess strong reagent commonly controls pH away from equivalence. At equivalence, the ideal spectator-ion solution is neutral relative to the temperature-dependent water equilibrium.
required_concepts: Excess strong acid/base determines off-equivalence behavior.
Neutrality at equivalence follows the water convention and ideal assumptions.
major_error_concepts: Calculating pH from the original acid concentration after ignoring neutralization and dilution.

cards.prompt: What is Weak Acid–Strong Base Titration? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A weak acid-strong base titration contains a buffer region before equivalence. At half-equivalence the ideal concentration-ratio approximation gives pH approximately pKa; at equivalence the conjugate base commonly makes the solution basic.
required_concepts: Buffer region and half-equivalence relation.
Conjugate-base hydrolysis at equivalence.
accepted_variants: Weak-acid neutralization with a strong-base titrant.
major_error_concepts: Assuming equivalence must occur at pH seven despite a basic conjugate ion.

cards.prompt: What is Acid–Base Indicator? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An acid-base indicator has differently colored acid and base forms whose ratio changes with pH. Its useful transition interval must align with the relevant titration's sharp pH change if it is to estimate equivalence well.
required_concepts: Conjugate forms differ in color.
Transition interval must suit the titration.
major_error_concepts: Assuming one indicator gives an accurate endpoint for every acid-base titration.

cards.prompt: What is Solubility Product? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A solubility product Ksp is the equilibrium activity product of ions for dissolution of a specified sparingly soluble solid. Stoichiometric exponents follow the dissolution equation, and Ksp is not generally equal to molar solubility.
required_concepts: Ion-activity product for dissolution.
Stoichiometry connects Ksp to solubility.
major_error_concepts: Equating Ksp numerically with molar solubility for every salt.

cards.prompt: What is Ion Product and Precipitation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The ion product Qsp uses current ionic activities in the solubility-product expression. Qsp>Ksp makes precipitation thermodynamically favored, Qsp<Ksp permits further dissolution if solid is available, and equality indicates saturation.
required_concepts: Compare current ion product with Ksp.
Kinetics and nucleation can delay visible precipitation.
major_error_concepts: Assuming Qsp>Ksp guarantees immediate visible solid formation regardless of nucleation barriers.

cards.prompt: What is Selective Precipitation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Selective precipitation exploits different solubility equilibria so one ion-containing solid becomes favored before another. Practical separation depends on concentrations, competing equilibria, and the required completeness, not Ksp ordering alone.
required_concepts: Differing precipitation thresholds enable separation.
Concentration and other equilibria matter.
major_error_concepts: Choosing the first precipitate solely by smallest Ksp when salt stoichiometries differ.

cards.prompt: What is Complex Ion? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A complex ion contains a central species, commonly a metal ion, coordinated by ligands donating electron pairs. Complex formation can change free-ion concentration and therefore other equilibria such as solubility.
required_concepts: Central species coordinated by electron-pair donor ligands.
Changes free-ion availability.
major_error_concepts: Assuming the total dissolved metal concentration equals its uncomplexed ion concentration.

cards.prompt: What is Formation Constant? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A formation constant Kf describes equilibrium formation of a specified complex from its components. Stepwise and overall constants correspond to different written reactions and combine multiplicatively when steps are added.
required_concepts: Equilibrium constant for the defined complex-formation reaction.
Distinguish stepwise and cumulative constants.
major_error_concepts: Comparing constants for different ligand stoichiometries as though they describe the same reaction.

cards.prompt: What is Entropy? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Entropy is a thermodynamic state function related to the number and distribution of accessible microscopic states. For reversible heat transfer, dS=delta q_rev/T; the slogan disorder is only a rough analogy.
required_concepts: State function linked to accessible microscopic states.
Reversible heat relation uses absolute temperature.
major_error_concepts: Treating visible messiness as a precise definition of entropy.

cards.prompt: What is Second Law of Thermodynamics? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The second law states that total entropy does not decrease for an isolated system, increasing in spontaneous irreversible processes. A subsystem's entropy can decrease if the surroundings' increase compensates.
required_concepts: Isolated total entropy is nondecreasing.
Subsystem decrease is allowed with appropriate exchange.
accepted_variants: The entropy criterion for spontaneous isolated change.
major_error_concepts: Claiming entropy must increase inside every individual subsystem at every moment.

cards.prompt: What is Third Law of Thermodynamics? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The third law assigns zero entropy to a perfect crystal with a unique ground state at zero kelvin in the standard formulation. Residual disorder or ground-state degeneracy requires qualification.
required_concepts: Perfect unique-ground-state crystal at zero kelvin.
Not every real material has zero residual entropy.
accepted_variants: The zero-temperature reference principle for entropy.
major_error_concepts: Claiming every substance has zero entropy at ordinary room temperature or regardless of residual disorder.

cards.prompt: What is Standard Molar Entropy? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Standard molar entropy is entropy per mole for a substance in its specified standard state at a stated temperature. Unlike standard formation enthalpies of elements, standard molar entropies of elements are not generally set to zero at room temperature.
required_concepts: Molar entropy at specified standard state and temperature.
Not assigned zero for all elements.
accepted_variants: S-degree for a mole of substance.
major_error_concepts: Setting every elemental standard molar entropy to zero by analogy with formation enthalpy.

cards.prompt: What is Gibbs Free Energy? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Gibbs free energy is G=H-TS. For a closed system at constant temperature and pressure under the appropriate constraints, spontaneous change lowers G and equilibrium minimizes it with respect to allowed changes.
required_concepts: G=H-TS.
Constant-temperature/pressure and allowed-process constraints matter.
accepted_variants: The free-energy potential for isothermal-isobaric equilibrium.
major_error_concepts: Using decrease of G as a universal criterion without considering constraints.

cards.prompt: What is Standard Free Energy and Equilibrium? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The standard reaction Gibbs energy satisfies delta G-degree=-RT ln K for a consistently defined dimensionless equilibrium constant. A large K corresponds to negative standard reaction free energy, not necessarily complete conversion under every starting condition.
required_concepts: Negative RT times natural log K.
Standard driving force differs from actual composition-dependent driving force.
accepted_variants: Thermodynamic link between standard free energy and equilibrium.
major_error_concepts: Using a positive sign in delta G-degree=RT ln K.

cards.prompt: What is Free Energy under Nonstandard Conditions? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Actual reaction free energy is delta G=delta G-degree+RT ln Q. At equilibrium Q=K and delta G=0, even when delta G-degree is nonzero.
required_concepts: Composition term RT ln Q.
Actual free-energy change vanishes at equilibrium.
major_error_concepts: Assuming equilibrium requires standard reaction free energy to be zero.

cards.prompt: What is Temperature and Spontaneity? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The relation delta G=delta H-T delta S explains how temperature can change thermodynamic favorability. Treating delta H and delta S as constant gives a useful limited-range approximation, not an exact rule over all temperatures or phase changes.
required_concepts: Enthalpy and entropy compete through temperature.
Constant-parameter assumption has a limited range.
accepted_variants: Temperature dependence of the free-energy balance.
major_error_concepts: Claiming every exothermic process is spontaneous at all temperatures regardless of entropy.

cards.prompt: What is Oxidation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Oxidation is loss of electrons or an increase in oxidation number in the relevant bookkeeping description. It occurs alongside reduction in a balanced redox process.
required_concepts: Electron loss or oxidation-number increase.
accepted_variants: The oxidative half of electron transfer.
major_error_concepts: Defining oxidation solely as addition of oxygen in every reaction.

cards.prompt: What is Reduction? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Reduction is gain of electrons or a decrease in oxidation number. In an overall redox reaction, electron gain is balanced by oxidation elsewhere.
required_concepts: Electron gain or oxidation-number decrease.
accepted_variants: The reductive half of electron transfer.
major_error_concepts: Reversing reduction and oxidation-number increase.

cards.prompt: What is Oxidation Number? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Oxidation number is the atomic charge obtained after an ionic approximation to bonding. For ordinary introductory Lewis structures, assign heteronuclear bond electrons to the more electronegative atom and split homonuclear bonds equally, then compare assigned electrons with those of the neutral atom. The numbers sum to the species charge. This is not a measured partial charge, and differs from formal charge, which splits all bond electrons equally. More advanced coordination cases may need the fuller electron-allegiance rule.
required_concepts: Describe ionic electron assignment: ordinary heteronuclear bonds go to the more electronegative partner, while identical-atom bonds split equally.
Distinguish oxidation number from actual partial charge and from the equal-sharing formal-charge convention.
accepted_variants: In ordinary CO2 bookkeeping, oxygen receives the C-O bonding electrons: O is -2 and C is +4, although the usual Lewis formal charges are zero.
major_error_concepts: Splitting every heteronuclear bond equally while calling the result an oxidation number.
Treating the assigned integer as a direct measurement of atomic partial charge.

cards.prompt: What is Oxidizing Agent? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An oxidizing agent causes another species to be oxidized while itself being reduced. It accepts electron equivalents in the overall bookkeeping.
required_concepts: Oxidizes the partner and is reduced itself.
major_error_concepts: Claiming the oxidizing agent is the species losing electrons.

cards.prompt: What is Reducing Agent? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A reducing agent causes another species to be reduced while itself being oxidized. It donates electron equivalents in the redox bookkeeping.
required_concepts: Reduces the partner and is oxidized itself.
major_error_concepts: Claiming the reducing agent gains electrons in the same overall process.

cards.prompt: What is Half-Reaction? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A half-reaction represents either oxidation or reduction with electrons shown explicitly. Combining properly balanced half-reactions cancels electrons and conserves atoms and charge in the net reaction.
required_concepts: One redox half with explicit electrons.
Combined equation conserves atoms and charge.
accepted_variants: An electron-balanced oxidation or reduction equation.
major_error_concepts: Leaving uncancelled electrons in a complete closed redox equation without an external electron source.

cards.prompt: What is Galvanic Cell? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A galvanic cell couples a spontaneous redox reaction to electrical work by separating oxidation and reduction spatially. Electrons flow through an external connection while ionic transport maintains charge balance.
required_concepts: Spontaneous redox drives electrical output.
Electron and ionic pathways have distinct roles.
major_error_concepts: Assuming the salt bridge is the ordinary path of external electron current.

cards.prompt: What is Electrolytic Cell? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: An electrolytic cell uses externally supplied electrical energy to drive a redox reaction that is nonspontaneous under the stated conditions. Oxidation still occurs at the anode and reduction at the cathode.
required_concepts: Electrical input drives the specified reaction.
Electrode reaction names do not reverse.
major_error_concepts: Claiming reduction moves to the anode simply because the cell is electrolytic.

cards.prompt: What is Anode? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The anode is the electrode where oxidation occurs. Its electrical sign depends on whether the device is operating galvanically or electrolytically, so sign alone is not the definition.
required_concepts: Oxidation electrode.
Sign depends on operating mode.
major_error_concepts: Defining the anode as always the positive electrode.

cards.prompt: What is Cathode? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The cathode is the electrode where reduction occurs. It is positive in the usual discharging galvanic-cell convention and negative in a simple driven electrolytic-cell convention, while its reduction role is invariant.
required_concepts: Reduction electrode.
Sign convention depends on operating mode.
major_error_concepts: Defining cathode by one fixed sign in all electrochemical devices.

cards.prompt: What is Salt Bridge? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A salt bridge or appropriate ionic connection permits charge-compensating ion transport between half-cells while limiting direct mixing. It completes the internal ionic circuit rather than carrying the external electron flow as free electrons.
required_concepts: Ionic charge balance between half-cells.
major_error_concepts: Describing the bridge as an electron wire.

cards.prompt: What is Standard Reduction Potential? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A standard reduction potential is the electrode potential for a specified reduction half-reaction relative to a reference electrode under standard-state conditions. Potentials are intensive and are not multiplied when a half-reaction is scaled.
required_concepts: Reference-relative reduction tendency under standard conditions.
Do not scale potential with coefficients.
major_error_concepts: Doubling an electrode potential because the half-reaction is multiplied by two.

cards.prompt: What is Cell Potential? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For a cell written with a cathodic reduction and anodic oxidation, standard cell potential is E-degree_cathode minus E-degree_anode when both tabulated values are reduction potentials. Reaction direction and conditions determine the sign.
required_concepts: Cathode reduction potential minus anode reduction potential.
Use consistent tabulated reduction conventions.
major_error_concepts: Adding two tabulated reduction potentials without reversing the anodic role.

cards.prompt: What is Nernst Equation? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The Nernst equation gives E=E-degree-(RT/(nF)) ln Q for the specified cell reaction. It relates potential to composition through a dimensionless reaction quotient; n is the electron stoichiometric count.
required_concepts: Subtract RT ln Q divided by nF.
Use the cell reaction's electron count and quotient.
major_error_concepts: Using total ion count rather than transferred electron count as n.

cards.prompt: What is Cell Potential and Free Energy? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Reaction free energy and reversible cell potential satisfy delta G=-nFE. Thus a positive potential for the written galvanic reaction corresponds to negative reaction free energy under the same conditions.
required_concepts: delta G=-nFE.
Consistent reaction direction and conditions.
accepted_variants: Electrical work and chemical free-energy relation.
major_error_concepts: Claiming positive cell voltage implies positive spontaneous reaction free energy.

cards.prompt: What is Faraday Constant? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: The Faraday constant is the charge magnitude per mole of elementary charges, equal to Avogadro's constant times the elementary charge. It converts between electron amount and electric charge.
required_concepts: Charge per mole of electrons in magnitude.
major_error_concepts: Confusing the Faraday constant with the charge of a single electron.

cards.prompt: What is Electrolysis Stoichiometry? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Electrolysis stoichiometry relates charge passed, Q=integral I dt, to electron amount Q/F and then to product amount through the balanced half-reaction. Actual yield can be lower when current efficiency is below one.
required_concepts: Charge to moles of electrons to reaction amount.
Account for current efficiency when relevant.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every mole of electrons always deposits one mole of metal regardless of ion charge.

cards.prompt: What is Corrosion? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Corrosion is material degradation through chemical or electrochemical interaction with the environment, often involving metal oxidation coupled to a reduction process elsewhere. Its rate depends on material, environment, and protective or galvanic effects.
required_concepts: Environment-driven material degradation.
Electrochemical coupling often drives metal corrosion.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every thermodynamically favorable corrosion reaction must proceed rapidly without kinetic barriers.

cards.prompt: What is Battery? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A battery stores chemical free energy and delivers electrical energy through one or more electrochemical cells. Rechargeable operation reverses suitable reactions with electrical input, but reversibility, capacity, and losses depend on the chemistry.
required_concepts: Chemical-to-electrical energy device.
Rechargeability requires suitable reversible operation.
major_error_concepts: Assuming every galvanic cell can be recharged safely and efficiently just by reversing current.

cards.prompt: What is Concentration Cell? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: A concentration cell obtains a potential difference from differing activities in otherwise related half-cell chemistry. The thermodynamic driving force is the tendency toward equilibration of chemical potential, captured by the Nernst relation.
required_concepts: Potential arises from an activity difference.
Same nominal electrode chemistry can still produce voltage.
major_error_concepts: Claiming identical electrode materials always imply zero voltage regardless of solution activities.

cards.prompt: What is Radioactive Decay? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Radioactive decay is spontaneous nuclear transformation governed statistically by a decay constant for a given nuclide and mode. The time of an individual event is unpredictable, while large populations follow a reproducible decay law.
required_concepts: Nuclear transformation with statistical population law.
Individual decay time is not predetermined by the simple rate description.
major_error_concepts: Treating radioactive decay as ordinary rearrangement of chemical bonds.

cards.prompt: What is Radioactive Half-Life? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: For a single radioactive decay mode with constant decay probability per unit time, half-life is ln 2 divided by the decay constant. Equal half-lives remove equal fractions, not equal numbers, of the remaining nuclei.
required_concepts: Constant fractional exponential decay.
Halving time relation.
accepted_variants: The time for half of an ensemble of parent nuclei to remain.
major_error_concepts: Assuming all nuclei must be gone after two half-lives.

cards.prompt: What is Fission and Fusion? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Nuclear fission splits a nucleus into smaller products, while fusion combines nuclei into a heavier product. Energy release depends on the change in binding energy per nucleon and the complete reaction, not merely on the labels splitting or joining.
required_concepts: Fission splits and fusion combines nuclei.
Energy balance depends on nuclear binding.
major_error_concepts: Claiming every imaginable fission or fusion reaction releases energy.

cards.prompt: What is Nuclear Binding Energy? State its defining idea and essential conditions.
cards.definition: Nuclear binding energy is the energy required to separate a nucleus into its constituent nucleons. The bound nucleus's mass is less than the sum of free constituent masses, with the mass difference related by E=mc squared.
required_concepts: Energy needed to separate bound nucleons.
Mass defect corresponds to binding energy.
accepted_variants: The energetic stability of a bound nucleus relative to free nucleons.
major_error_concepts: Equating nuclear binding energy with the chemical bond energy between atoms.

description: A definition-recall course deck covering core concepts in General Chemistry II.
